NRBS 3410
Summer 2026
Sexually Transmitted Infections

STI Definition
 STI (formally known as STD)
 Infection of reproductive tract by microorganism
through vaginal, oral or anal sexual activity.
 65 million individuals have incurable STI (herpes, HIV)
 19 million new STIs diagnosed annually
 Women disproportionately affected and have greater morbidity 
associated with STIs.
 In some cultures-having an STI may negatively affect a woman’s 
standing in the communities with high value on virginity
 Leading some women to avoid even the discussion of testing.

Groups at High Risk for STIs
 66% of all STIs are diagnosed in those under 25.
5 million adolescents diagnosed each year. 
Adolescents engage in high risk behaviors due to emotional 
immaturity
 Lower rates of condom use
 Inappropriate condom use/storage
 Higher number of sexual partners
 Inability to discuss sexual activity
In the US highest risk of adolescent STIs are in
African Americans
Abused/homeless
Gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgendered youths

Factors Placing Teenagers at Risk for STIs
 Females’ anatomy predisposing them to STIs 
(vaginal columnar epithelial cells extend out 
over cervix=more susceptible)
 Teenagers’ feelings of invincibility
 Higher rates of unprotected intercourse
 Obstacles to using the health care system
 Most states do not require parental consent for 
reproductive health care (Utah & Texas exceptions)
 Reluctance to discuss sexual practices
 Partnerships of limited duration=increased 
number of partners=increased risk for STI

Sexually Transmitted Infections 
Characterized by Vaginal Discharge
Vaginitis- inflammation or infection of vagina.  
 Candida-NOT a true STI- 75% of women have at least 1 episode
 Fungal infection AKA “yeast” infection
 Normal vaginal microbiota is responsible for pH of vaginal secretions that promote environment 
hospitable to sperm
 Imbalances in vagina lead to proliferation of pathogenic organisms
Nursing care: Prevention and Treatment
Wear cotton underwear, avoid tight fitting artificial fibers, change wet bathing suits ASAP
Wipe front to back, avoid douches, powders and vaginal sprays. Avoid bubble baths.
Use condoms-prevents spread of more pathogenic organisms
Treatment available OTC
Intravaginal- Miconaizole suppository or cream (Monistat)
1 day- 1200 mcg/3 day 200 mcg/7day 100 mcg 
Oral- Diflucan single 150mg tab – needs prescription
During pregnancy-can be transmitted to neonate during delivery causing oral candidiasis “thrush”

Candidiasis Symptoms & Risk Factors
Symptoms-may worsen pre-
menstrually
Pruritus-itching of vulva or 
vagina
Thick white discharge “cottage 
cheese like”
Vaginal soreness
Vulvar burning
Erythema of vulvovaginal tissue
Dispareunia
External dysuria
Risk Factors
 Pregnancy: hormonal 
changes affect normal flora
 Hormonal contraception use
 Broad spectrum antibiotic 
use
 Diabetes
 Obesity
 Steroid or 
immunosuppressant use
 HIV infection
 Wearing tight clothing
 Chemical irritant or trauma to 
vaginal tissue

Trichomoniasis
Trichomoniasis-protozoa
 Sexually transmitted
 Men are asymptomatic
 Female symptoms vary
 Heavy grey/yellow frothy 
 Foul smelling discharge
 Vulvovaginal 
pruritis/soreness/erythema
 Cervix bleeds on contact
Diagnosed with microscopy
Treatment: Abstain from sex until 
both treated
Women: Metronidazole 500 mg 2 
times/day for 7 days
Men: Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single 
dose
TOC- test of cure recommended @ 
3months
Increased risk for LBW infant in 
pregnancy
Bacterial Vaginosis Gardnerella-bacterium
Sexually associated infection: can occur 
without sex
Low numbers of normal flora: lactobacillus in 
vagina 
 Thin white discharge with distinct “stale 
fish” odor
 Vaginal pH > 4.5
 50% of women are asymptomatic
Diagnosis 3 of 4 criteria : “whiff test” 10% 
potassium hydroxide = fish smell, clue 
cell (vaginal epithelium cell covered in 
bacteria), pH & notable discharge
 Metronidazole 500 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 
days
 OR
 Metronidazole gel 0.75% one full applicator (5 
g) intravaginally, once a day for 5 days
 OR
 Clindamycin cream 2% one full applicator (5 g) 
intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days
Partner not treated
Associated with preterm labor, 
chorioamnionitis, post partum infections 
and PID

Bacterial Vaginosis BV
Bacterial Vaginosis Gardnerella-bacterium
Sexually associated infection: can occur without sex
Low numbers of normal flora: lactobacillus in vagina 
Thin white discharge with distinct “stale fish” odor
Vaginal pH > 4.5
50% of women are asymptomatic
Diagnosis 3 of 4 criteria : “whiff test” 10% potassium hydroxide = fish smell, clue 
cell (vaginal epithelium cell covered in bacteria), pH & notable discharge
Metronidazole 500 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days
OR
Metronidazole gel 0.75% one full applicator (5 g) intravaginally, once a day for 5 
days
OR
Clindamycin cream 2% one full applicator (5 g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 
days
Partner not treated
Associated with preterm labor, chorioamnionitis, post partum 
infections and PID

Chlamydia (C.Trachomatis)
 Most common STI in US- 2.8 million cases 
 Highest among ages 15-19 yrs
 50% of women 70% of men are asymptomatic
 Men may present with urethritis.
 Women-pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility
 Causes over 50% of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
 20-30% of chlamydia patients untreated get PID
 10% of women with PID will have tubal infertility
 vaginal discharge, endocervicitis, inflammations of the rectum and lining of the eye, can infect 
throat
 Routine testing of all sexually active women under 25.
 Diagnosis by clean catch urine sample or vaginal swab culture
Treatment
 Doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days or
 Oral Azithromycin 1 Gram single dose or
 Levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days
 Test of Cure (TOC) repeated testing 2-3 wks post treatment in pregnant women.
 May cause conjunctivitis in neonate

Gonorrhea
 2nd most reported infection in US
 700,000 new cases annually- required reporting to 
Health Department
 Increased risk for HIV, PID, infertility, ectopic preg.:
 may be asymptomatic, dysuria, urinary frequency, 
vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, endocervicitis, 
arthritis, PID, rectal infection
 Diagnosed-vaginal or urethral swab culture.
 Patients infected with N. gonorrhoeae frequently are 
coinfected with Chlamydia 
Treatment-Single dose 500 mg Ceftriaxone IM or if 
co-infection with chlamydia add Doxycycline 100mg PO 
2x day
Drug resistance- quinolone resistant strains rampant.
 Neonates are treated with Erythromycin ointment at 
birth to prevent blindness associated with Gonorrhea

HSV: Genital Herpes
 Herpes Simplex Virus- Type I 
not sexually transmitted, Type 
II: sexually transmitted.
 No cure
 Contact with mucous 
membranes with active lesions
 Affects 50 million in the US
 80% of infected people 
aren’t aware of infection
 Blister-like genital lesions, 
dysuria, fever, headache, 
muscle aches
 After initial outbreak-virus 
lies dormant-may be 
triggered by illness, stress, 
pregnancy, medications
Neonatal birth transmission is
30-50% with active lesions.

HSV Treatment
Acute Infection
 Acyclovir† 400 mg orally 3 
times/day for 7–10 days
OR
Famciclovir 250 mg orally 3 
times/day for 7–10 days
OR
Valacyclovir 1 gm orally 2 
times/day for 7–10 days
 * Treatment can be extended if 
healing is incomplete after 10 
days of therapy.
 †Acyclovir 200 mg orally five 
times/day is also effective but is 
not recommended because of the 
frequency of dosing.
Suppressive Treatment
Recurrent HSV/Partner Discordant
 Acyclovir 400 mg orally 2 times/day
OR
Valacyclovir 500 mg orally once a 
day*
OR
Valacyclovir 1 gm orally once a day
OR
Famciclovir 250 mg orally 2 
times/day
 * Valacyclovir 500 mg once a day 
might be less effective than other 
valacyclovir or acyclovir dosing 
regimens for persons who have 
frequent recurrences (i.e., ≥10 
episodes/year).

Syphilis
Caused by spirochete: Treponema Pallidum
Crosses the placenta: 2.1 million women have active syphilis-
causes poor outcome in pregnancy: abortion, still-birth, multi-
symptom organ failure 
Five Stages: 
 Primary: chancre on place of bacteria entrance
 Secondary: maculopapular rash, sore throat, 
lymphadenopathy, flu-like symptoms
 Early Latent-still contagious decrease symptoms
 Latent: no symptoms; no longer contagious
 Tertiary: tumors of the skin, bones, and liver, CNS 
symptoms, CV symptoms; usually not reversible
Diagnosis-serology rapid plasma regain  (RPR) and Venereal 
Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL )
Treatment-Penicillin G IM/IV 2.4 million units single dose
Doxycycline, tetracycline or Ceftriaxone if allergic

HPV Human Papilloma Virus: Genital Warts
 HPV-Most common viral infection in US
 5.5 million new cases annually
 Nearly all sexually active men (90%) and 
women (80%) will get it in their lifetime
 Causes 90% of anal and cervical cancers, 
70% of vaginal and vulvar cancers, 60% 
of penile cancer
 Most cases are sub-clinical. Most people do 
not know 
 Wart-like lesions that are soft, moist, or 
flesh-colored may appear on the vulva and 
cervix, vagina,  anus, or penis.
 Most resolve within 2 years without 
treatment
 Treatment:
 Cryotherapy to “freeze” warts, 
surgical/laser or electrosurgery to remov
 Topicals: Podofilox or Imiquimod gel x 4 
weeks

HPV Vaccine Gardasil
 Vaccine against HPV Types 6,11, 16, and 18
CDC recommendation: Series of 3 vaccinations over 6 
months (2 months apart) May continue with series even if 
interrupted 
All children between 11-12 years (can start at 9)
Young women under 25, men under 21
Studies show immunity lasting at least 10 yrs

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease PID 
 Result of ascending polymicrobial infection of upper female 
reproductive tract 
 750,000 cases annually
 Frequently from untreated chlamydia or gonorrhea
 Complications-10-15% of women become infertile
 Therapeutic Management
 IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
 Oral fluids
 Bed rest
 Pain management-analgesics
 Education to prevent recurrence 
 
Manifestations: lower abdominal tenderness, adnexal 
tenderness, cervical motion tenderness
Diagnosis: endometrial biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound, 
laparoscopic examination

Hepatitis A, B & C
 Hepatitis A spread via GI tract NOT an STI
 Hepatitis B via saliva, blood, semen, menstrual 
blood, and vaginal secretions. 
 Hepatitis C is not sexually transmitted unless 
actively ill.  Hep C carriers don’t transmit 
sexually.
 Treatments to cure available now
 Hep B- Prevention through immunization.

Ectoparasite Infections
 Scabies: intensely pruritic dermatitis with 
lesions
 Pubic lice: pruritus with lice or nits
 Treatment: permethrin cream or lindane 
shampoo; decontamination of bedding and 
clothing; treatment of family members and 
sexual partners
 3-tiered approach: eradicate infestation, remove 
nits, prevent spread or recurrence
 Education on prevention and treatment

Human Immunodeficiency Virus: HIV
HIV attacks and destroys the infection-fighting CD4 cells (CD4 T lymp
hocyte) of the immune system. Loss of CD4 cells makes it hard for 
the body to fight off infections and certain HIV-related cancers.
15% of people with HIV don’t know they have it
Most at risk for HIV
 People who have unprotected sex with multiple partners.
 Healthcare workers who may come in contact with bodily fluids.
 People who travel to areas where HIV is common (such as sub-
Saharan Africa).

HIV Testing and Risks
CDC recommends: Everyone ages 13 to 64 should get tested for HIV at 
least once as part of routine health care.
People with certain risk factors should get tested more often. You should get 
tested at least once a year if:
• You're a man who has sex with another man.
• You've had anal or vaginal sex with someone who has HIV.
• You've had more than one sex partner since your last HIV test.
• You've shared needles, syringes, or other drug injection equipment (for 
example, cookers).
• You've exchanged sex for drugs or money.
• You've been diagnosed with or treated for another sexually transmitted 
infection, hepatitis, or tuberculosis (TB).
• You've had sex with someone who has done anything listed above or you 
don't know their sexual history.

HIV Tests
 The rapid antigen/antibody test, done with blood from a 
finger stick, takes 30 minutes or less. Healthcare 
Institutions/LABS
 With a rapid antibody test, usually done with blood from a 
finger stick or with oral fluid, results are ready in 30 minutes 
or less. This includes HIV self-tests used at home or in a 
private location. 
 Nucleic Acid Test (NAT) presence of actual virus in blood
It may take several days for test results with a Nucleic Acid 
Test (NAT) or antigen/antibody lab test. 
 At home HIV self-tests available
 Must follow directions EXACTLY for accuracy

HIV continued
 Transmission through semen or vaginal secretions
 Fetal and neonatal effects: immunocompromised infant
 HIV and adolescents increasing; most exposed via 
sexual intercourse
 HIV rates increasing in adolescents and elderly
 Manifestations: acute phase; asymptomatic with viral 
replication, immunosuppression with opportunistic 
infections

HIV continued
Therapeutic management: Aniti-retroviral Therapy (ART)
 Multiple drugs on the market
 Prep: prevents infection 
 Goal: undetectable viral load = not transmissible through 
sex 
 Once HIV treatment is started, it usually takes 3 to 6 
months for a person’s viral load to reach an undetectable 
level. 
Nursing management
 Education about drug therapy
 Compliance & frequent testing
 Prevention
 Care during pregnancy and childbirth
 Referrals

HIV & Pregnancy
 Pregnant people with HIV should take antiretroviral therapy (ART) 
throughout pregnancy and childbirth to prevent perinatal transmission of 
HIV. Lowers risk of transmission to <1%
 Pregnant people with HIV can have vaginal deliveries.  
 High viral load (more than 1,000 copies/mL) or an unknown viral load 
near the time of delivery, a scheduled C-section reduces the risk of 
transmission
 Neonates should receive ART to reduce the risk of developing HIV. 
 For newborns at low-risk of perinatal HIV (mother took art)
 2-week zidovudine (ZDV) ARV regimen is recommended for ARV 
prophylaxis if the newborn is ≥37 weeks gestation
 HIV may be passed through in breastmilk in untreated individuals
 HOWEVER: Breastfeeding is safe (less than 1% risk) with the following
 Patient has been taking ART therapy and had an undetectable viral 
load during pregnancy 
 Continues on ART while breastfeeding

Preventing STIs
 Education about safer sex practices
 Behavior modification
 Contraception
